content: Injury is a significant and growing global cause of death and disability. To address this, new trauma care models have been developed. While many of these models were initially created in high-income countries (HICs), they are now being implemented in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). One such model is the advanced trauma life support (ATLS) training program for hospital staff, which is being promoted in LMICs as a strategy to improve outcomes for trauma victims. However, the effectiveness of this intervention has not been rigorously evaluated through systematic reviews in either HIC or LMIC settings. The objective of this study was to measure the impact of ATLS training for hospital staff on injury-related mortality and morbidity in hospitals that have implemented such training programs compared to those that have not. A comprehensive search for relevant studies was conducted on May 16, 2014. The databases searched included the Cochrane Injuries Group's Specialised Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, ISI Web of Science, CINAHL Plus, and PubMed. Additionally, reference lists of identified studies were screened. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials, controlled trials, and controlled before-and-after studies that compared the outcomes of hospitals with ATLS-trained staff to those without such training. Three authors independently applied these criteria to the identified studies and extracted data. The search did not identify any studies that met the inclusion criteria for this review. As a result, no evidence from controlled trials was available to determine whether ATLS or similar programs improve outcomes for trauma victims. While there is some evidence suggesting that educational initiatives like ATLS improve hospital staff's knowledge of emergency interventions, there is no evidence to suggest that trauma management systems incorporating ATLS training lead to better outcomes for patients. The authors concluded that there is currently no controlled trial evidence to support the effectiveness of ATLS training in improving outcomes for trauma victims. Future research should focus on evaluating trauma systems that incorporate ATLS training, both at the hospital level and within broader health systems, using more rigorous research designs.
